idiom_name: small wrapper struct implementing the locally owned interface
implementation_notes: Go satisfies interfaces implicitly, so there is no declaration to inherit and no adapter framework to reach for: define the target interface in the package that consumes it, keep it small, then write a struct (or a function type) that implements it by translating each call to the dependency. Embedding an adaptee promotes its whole method set and is usually the wrong tool here - an explicit field keeps only the interface methods visible and makes the boundary obvious. Single-method interfaces are so common that a named function type with the method attached is the idiomatic short form; the standard library does exactly this with http.HandlerFunc and adapts low-level implementations to shared interfaces throughout package io.
pitfalls: Embedding the adaptee promotes all of its methods, so the adapter exposes an interface wider than the target and callers start depending on the vendor API again.

Typed-nil trap: assigning a nil *Adapter to an interface produces a non-nil interface value, so `if service == nil` does not detect the nil pointer; reject it in the constructor or return a nil interface.
An adapter whose dependency is nil still satisfies the interface; validate in the constructor and return an error so the failure appears at wiring time, not at first use.
Defining the interface in the provider's package couples the adapter to the provider's vocabulary - the consumer owns the interface.

variants.name: Named function type adapted to the interface
variants.implementation_notes: When the target interface has exactly one method - the common Go case - a named function type implements it: `type NotifierFunc func(string) error` with a Notify method adapts any ordinary function to the interface, precisely how http.HandlerFunc adapts a function to http.Handler. Use it for stateless translation; keep the struct wrapper when the adapter needs configuration, logging, error normalisation or more than one method.
variants.idiom_name: type ClockFunc func() time.Time with a Now() method
pitfalls: A nil function value still satisfies the interface and panics when called - validate before assigning it.
Function types carry no state: configuration must arrive through a closure capture, which turns it back into a lightweight struct in disguise.
Method values and bound methods can allocate; wrapping in a hot loop trades allocation for readability.
